Un combat pour une chaîne de télé consac: A fight for a TV channel dedicated to diversity
Le Québec a-t-il besoin d’une chaîne de: Does Quebec need a television channel dedicated to ethnocultural diversity?
Jean-Yves Roux, fondateur et directeur g: Jean-Yves Roux, founder and general manager of Natyf TV Photo: Félix Lacerte-Gauthier
Le Québec a-t-il besoin d’une chaîne de: Does Quebec need a television channel dedicated to ethnocultural diversity? That is the question the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) must now consider, as Natyf TV pursues an application to be included in mandatory distribution in the province.
En ondes depuis 2018, la chaîne est « ax: On the air since 2018, the channel is “focused on diversity and on discovering the different cultures of racialized communities,” and its programming is mainly dedicated to the Black community. However, it has limited reach and limited means, a situation its founder wants to change.
« Présentement, Natyf TV a un statut de: “Right now, Natyf TV has the status of a specialty channel. It's a channel that a person has to subscribe to on their own. Among the big national cable distributors, the only one that has agreed to do business with us and carry us is Bell,” says Jean-Yves Roux, founder and general manager of Natyf TV.
Et ce n’est pas faute d’avoir essayé. Au: And it's not for lack of trying. Over the past few years, his team has, by his account, repeatedly tried to convince other major players, including Vidéotron and Cogeco, to carry Natyf TV. Without success. “Cable distributors aren't just cable distributors. They also own specialty and general-interest television channels. It's a huge media monopoly,” Roux points out.
Tanné de se buter à des portes closes, i: Tired of running into closed doors, he put his “plan B” into action, starting talks with the CRTC in 2020 to change the channel's status. “When we approached the CRTC, we realized that the mandate we had given ourselves at the start could be considered an essential mandate for Canadian and Quebec society. Then it took two years to get through the whole process, until the fall of 2022,” Roux says. Those efforts led, on January 10, to a Commission hearing to review Natyf TV's application. The CRTC is expected to issue its decision in the coming months.
Le changement de statut permettrait à Na: The change in status would allow Natyf TV to be part of the mandatory distribution in the basic subscription package, alongside TV5, AMI-télé, ARTV and TVA.
La redevance mensuelle demandée est de 0: The monthly fee being requested is $0.12. It would be paid to Natyf TV for every subscriber to a television service in the province. “It would give us an interesting financial cushion, but above all it would give us access to millions of potential viewers. With that many subscribers, it would open doors for us and give us access to much more attractive advertising budgets from advertisers,” Roux explains.
Entrepreneur et producteur, Kevin Calixt: Entrepreneur and producer Kevin Calixte, for his part, believes that with a bigger budget, Natyf TV could help develop new talent and offer them opportunities they don't have elsewhere. “They all say diversity is important to them, but at the end of the day, it's still the same team, the same technicians, the same producers. There may be more representation of the community [in front of the camera], but the story is still written by the same people,” says Calixte, who also hosts his own talk show, which has aired on the channel since 2020.
Il rappelle d’ailleurs que, si les chaîn: He also points out that if traditional television channels are struggling to compete with streaming platforms like Netflix, it is partly because they don't offer enough original stories that interest viewers. “For the general public, it would mean different content. A chance to come at television with a different approach. Some regions are less diverse, but it gives them the chance to follow a story with another approach and new faces,” Calixte believes.
Il n’est toutefois pas certain que le CR: However, it is not certain that the CRTC will approve the change in status Natyf TV is seeking. Several major players have spoken publicly to ask it to reject the application, including Vidéotron, Cogeco, TV5 and Rogers. In a joint letter filed in the record, Susan Wheeler, Vice-President, Regulatory Affairs, Media, at Rogers Media, along with Sam Norouzi, Vice-President and General Manager of ICI Télévision, argue that “Natyf's application does not meet the burden of proof and should be denied.”
Pour soutenir leur affirmation, ils décl: In support of their claim, they state that the channel has not provided a study or survey to back up its application. They also question how it could manage to meet its commitments on local content. And they argue that Natyf TV's advertising revenue projections are “too optimistic,” and that the channel has an “unrealistic view of the current state of the advertising market.” “While Natyf's intentions are laudable, we fail to see how, exactly, it will reach such ambitious levels of independent production programming,” they write.
Ils rappellent en outre que la distribut: They also point out that mandatory distribution would affect broadcasting distribution undertakings, which are required to offer their basic service at a maximum price of $25 per month. “[Natyf TV] has not shown that it has the expertise, the infrastructure, the partnerships with producers and advertisers, and the financial stability to meet its commitments. For these reasons, we do not believe the proposed business plan is viable,” they conclude.
Pour sa part, Marie-Philippe Bouchard, p: For her part, Marie-Philippe Bouchard, President and CEO of TV5 Québec Canada, states in a letter she sent to the CRTC that there would be “some overlap” between her channel's mandate and “Natyf TV's aspirations.” “We were surprised to see that Natyf TV mentions a multitude of optional French-language services, stressing that none of them meets the needs of cultural communities seeking to see themselves on Quebec francophone television, yet never mentions the existence of TV5/Unis TV, whose mandate is to promote the Francophonie, across all cultural communities,” she writes.
Vice-président des Affaires réglementair: Paul Beaudry, Vice-President of Regulatory Affairs at Cogeco, also believes that the role Natyf TV is seeking is already filled by TV5 and OMNI. He further insists that on-screen diversity is already reflected in the regular programming of general-interest television channels. “[Natyf] has failed to demonstrate that mandatory distribution – an extraordinary and exceptional measure used sparingly by the Commission – is warranted in this proceeding,” he told the CRTC in English.
Québecor Média, au nom de Vidéotron, s’o: Quebecor Media, on behalf of Vidéotron, also opposes the channel's application, stating that Natyf TV does not meet the criteria and that granting a mandatory distribution order would create a “dangerous precedent.” The company, too, argues that other channels already fill the role being requested.
« Nous soumettons respectueusement que N: “We respectfully submit that Natyf TV does not add value to Vidéotron's offering given its programming and generates little interest among Vidéotron subscribers, which explains our refusal to carry it in the past. […] Its inclusion in the basic service therefore appears all the more unjustified,” Peggy Tabet, Vice-President, Regulatory and Environmental Affairs at Quebecor, stated in a brief submitted to the CRTC.
Natyf TV n’a cependant pas que des oppos: But Natyf TV doesn't have only opponents. Several public figures and organizations have come out in favour of its application.
Quatre élus municipaux, dont Gracia Kaso: Four municipal elected officials, including Gracia Kasoki Katahwa, mayor of the Côte-des-Neiges–Notre-Dame-de-Grâce borough, have written to the CRTC to support its application.
« En tant que première femme noire maire: “As the first Black woman to be a borough mayor in the City of Montréal, I share a common mission with Natyf TV: to offer better representation of cultural communities seeking recognition,” she stated, among other things.
Plusieurs organismes et associations, do: Several organizations and associations, including the Michaëlle Jean Foundation, the Fédération africaine canadienne de l'économie (FACE) and the Coalition M.É.D.I.A, have also supported the application, as has businesswoman Fabienne Colas. “Bringing this project to life would give the growing number of creators from cultural diversity the chance to produce and broadcast quality content aimed at an audience seeking recognition and representation in the media,” Mylène Augustin and Joan Jenkinson, representing Black on Black Films and the Black Screen Office respectively, wrote in a joint letter.
Cofondatrice de la Fondation Dynastie, C: Carla Beauvais, co-founder of the Fondation Dynastie, draws on her own experience to explain what the television channel could bring. “Since the beginnings of the Gala Dynastie in 2017, it's always been a dream for us to be broadcast. For several years now, we've approached every possible broadcaster, but so far, we've never had a positive answer,” she says. That will change this year, as the Gala will air on Natyf TV.
Mme Beauvais estime que d’autres product: Beauvais believes other producers are in the same situation and struggle a great deal to get broadcast. A member of various juries, including that of the Canada Media Fund, she is aware of the issues this raises. “When you have a broadcaster attached, it helps a lot in getting different sources of funding for TV or film content. Often, people can't even get to the stage of submitting their project because they don't have a broadcaster,” she says.
Elle réfute également l’argument selon l: She also rejects the argument that other channels, including OMNI, already fill the same role. “Other channels give a lot of space to diversity, but not in French. The difference with Natyf is that it's a francophone channel. It's not a channel for immigrants who want to watch content in Spanish, Creole or Mandarin.”
Professeur à l’École des médias de l’UQA: Patrick White, a professor at UQAM's École des médias, doubts that Natyf TV's application will get it the results it expects. “Getting mandatory distribution doesn't mean much anymore in 2023, when many Canadians are cancelling cable and moving to streaming platforms,” he says.
À ses yeux, la chaîne devrait plutôt tra: In his view, the channel should instead work on “another multiplatform strategy” to build its audience. “There would be tangible benefits to having Natyf TV in the television landscape, but TFO, Radio-Canada, TV5 and Unis already play a leading role among francophones,” he adds.
Le professeur ajoute que la chaîne est «: The professor adds that the channel is “very little known,” which could work against it. “Unfortunately, Natyf TV's application to the CRTC for mandatory distribution of the channel seems quite futile,” he believes.
Malgré tout, M. Roux, le fondateur et di: Despite it all, Roux, Natyf TV's founder and general manager, is hopeful that the CRTC will grant his application. “It's as if the stars are aligned right now. Too many elements have come together for it not to be obvious that the mandate we're asking for would be useful to Quebec society,” he confides.
Si jamais il essuie un refus, il prévoit: If he is turned down, he still plans to pursue his development plan for the channel to grow its audience. “Of course, without a licence, we won't have certain resources. We'll have to keep looking here and there to make a little headway. It'll be much harder to reach our development goals. Impossible, no, but harder,” he says.
<strong>Une chaîne encore jeune</strong>: A channel still in its early years
C’est en 2018 que la chaîne est entrée e: The channel went on the air in 2018, first under the name CNVTV (for Channel New Victory), whose “inspirational content focused on family and spirituality” also made room for cultural communities.
« Pendant les premiers mois, on remarqua: “During the first few months, we noticed that people weren't managing to understand our positioning and even had trouble remembering the channel's name. We had no choice but to go back to the drawing board,” recalls Jean-Yves Roux, the channel's founder and general manager.
Après un long processus, le changement d: After a long process, the name change to Natyf TV became official in January 2019, and the channel's focus shifted to content dedicated to ethnic communities.
L’essentiel du contenu actuellement diff: Most of the content currently broadcast on the channel is not Canadian, and is imported notably from Africa and France. “We have no choice but to operate that way. Our long-term goal is to develop local talent. But you need the financial means to do that,” Roux explains. That situation would be reversed if the CRTC approved the licence change. Natyf TV wants to reorient its programming to serve Quebec's “Black, Arab, Hispanic and South Asian” communities. Various projects to that end are reportedly in development.
